record.title: LungIMPACT randomized trial finds no significant pathway-time benefit from immediate AI prioritization of primary-care chest X-rays
record.summary: The prospective, multicentre LungIMPACT randomized controlled trial compared immediate qXR AI worklist prioritization with usual reporting for adult primary-care chest X-rays across five NHS trusts in England. AI decision support was available in both arms; the randomized intervention was when the AI alert arrived. Of 97,731 CXRs, 93,326 were analyzed. The peer-reviewed report found no statistically significant difference in time to CT (median 53 days in both groups) or lung-cancer diagnosis (44 versus 46 days), and no significant differences in referral, treatment timing or stage at diagnosis. This is a bounded result about immediate worklist prioritization in this trial context, not a comparison of AI with no AI or evidence that all AI imaging uses lack value.
organizations: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: LungIMPACT was a prospective multicentre randomized trial of immediate AI prioritization for primary-care-requested chest X-rays; the report states 97,731 CXRs were collected and 93,326 analyzed across five NHS trusts in England.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The published trial report says immediate qXR worklist prioritization did not significantly change time to CT or lung-cancer diagnosis: median time to CT was 53 days in both arms, and median time to diagnosis was 44 versus 46 days. The authors also report no significant differences in referral timing, treatment timing or stage at diagnosis.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: AI decision support was available in both arms and the intervention was the timing of the AI alert; the trial therefore does not compare AI support with no AI support.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The result does not establish whether broader NHS chest-X-ray AI deployments, different algorithms, different clinical pathways or other AI uses improve patient outcomes; their identity with the trial intervention is unresolved.

evidence_gaps.description: The full peer-reviewed article and supplement were not inspectable in this activation; PubMed abstract and registry record were accessible.

The trial tests timing of qXR alerts, whereas broader NHS usage and outcome figures cited in the Oct 24 UK government package do not name a system, cohort or source. Identity and transfer are unknown.
No independent reanalysis or participant-level dataset inspection was performed; the registry says individual participant data are not intended to be shared.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported randomized result is reliable, it changes clinical workflow and procurement decisions for AI-assisted chest-X-ray prioritization in the tested lung-cancer pathway. The importance is substantial but bounded to immediate qXR alert timing in participating English NHS trusts; it does not establish that AI image analysis has no value in other workflows or uses.
limitations: This is one trial of immediate qXR worklist prioritization in a specific English primary-care pathway, not a test of all AI imaging tools or AI versus no AI.
The publication's abstract reports no statistically significant primary-outcome differences; this is not proof of exact equivalence or absence of smaller effects.
The full article and supplement were not accessible through the available reader in this activation, and independent reanalysis was not performed.

The 24 Oct 2026 UK government AI package separately cites broader NHS chest-X-ray AI metrics without naming a system or linking a dataset. The available evidence does not establish that those metrics describe the LungIMPACT intervention or population, so they are not treated as a direct contradiction or merged with this event.

brief.summary: The prospective, multicentre LungIMPACT randomized controlled trial compared immediate qXR AI worklist prioritization with usual reporting for adult primary-care chest X-rays across five NHS trusts in England. AI decision support was available in both arms; the randomized intervention was when the AI alert arrived. Of 97,731 CXRs, 93,326 were analyzed. The peer-reviewed report found no statistically significant difference in time to CT (median 53 days in both groups) or lung-cancer diagnosis (44 versus 46 days), and no significant differences in referral, treatment timing or stage at diagnosis. This is a bounded result about immediate worklist prioritization in this trial context, not a comparison of AI with no AI or evidence that all AI imaging uses lack value.

technical.claimed_result: The trial authors report no statistically significant effect of immediate AI prioritization on time to CT or lung-cancer diagnosis. The reported median time to CT was 53 days in each arm; median time to diagnosis was 44 days with prioritization and 46 days without. The report also says referral timing, treatment timing and stage at diagnosis did not differ significantly.
technical.compute_or_cost: The accessible abstract and registry do not report model-inference compute or a cost-effectiveness result.
technical.demonstrated_result: The journal report and PubMed record establish that a prospective multicentre randomized trial was conducted and published. The ISRCTN registry prospectively describes randomizing the timing of qXR alerts while making AI support available in both arms.
technical.implementation_status: The trial is reported as completed and its results were published in Nature Medicine in March 2026. The registry states that qXR was already in routine clinical use in some NHS trusts; this study evaluated immediate alert timing, not the effect of introducing AI versus no AI.
technical.mechanism: qXR AI decision support was available to clinicians for chest X-rays in both study arms. On randomized intervention days an immediate AI alert prioritized suspicious studies for review; on routine days the AI result was available at usual reporting time. Clinicians retained the decision about further imaging and referrals.
technical.novelty: The randomized design tests an operational workflow intervention and patient-pathway outcomes at scale, while keeping AI support available in both arms. The result is specific to immediate qXR prioritization and should not be recast as a general test of AI image interpretation.
technical.regime: Adults with primary-care-requested anteroposterior or posteroanterior chest X-rays in five NHS trusts in England; trial imaging ran July 2023–December 2024. qXR AI support was available in both groups, with immediate worklist prioritization randomized by day.
technical.reproducibility: The article is peer-reviewed and the trial was prospectively registered as ISRCTN78987039. The full-text page was blocked in this activation; only the PubMed abstract and registry record were inspected. Independent reanalysis and participant-level data access were not established.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within-trial routine-reporting days in which the same qXR AI output remained available to the reporting clinician at usual reporting time; this isolates the timing/prioritization intervention more closely than an AI-versus-no-AI comparison.

brief.title: LungIMPACT randomized trial finds no significant pathway-time benefit from immediate AI prioritization of primary-care chest X-rays
brief.why_it_matters: The trial tests whether moving AI alerts earlier in a real diagnostic workflow improves patient-pathway outcomes, rather than whether a model can detect abnormalities in isolation. Its reported null primary outcomes show that faster AI-supported image review alone did not significantly shorten CT or diagnosis times in the studied pathway. Deployment evaluation should therefore distinguish image analysis, alert timing and downstream clinical workflow, while avoiding generalization beyond the tested qXR and English primary-care setting.
